study.title: 2 Corinthians 5 - future hope, life by faith and ministry of reconciliation
study.overview: In this chapter, Paul unites comfort and responsibility. He speaks of the hope of the resurrection and an eternal indwelling given by God, showing that the present life is marked by groaning, weakness and faith, not by immediate vision. This hope does not lead to passivity, but to a life that pleases the Lord, because we will all appear before Christ. Paul then explains that Christ's love moves him in his ministry: the death of Jesus defines a new way of knowing people, produces a new creation in whom he is in Christ and sustains the central message of reconciliation. The climax of the chapter is the statement that God in Christ dealt with sin in a decisive way so that sinners were made righteousness of God.

outline.title: Hope of an eternal indwelling
outline.explanation: Paul contrasts the mortal body, called a tabernacle, with the eternal indwelling prepared by God. The groaning of the believer are not a desire to escape from life, but longing for the coating of glorified life. The Spirit is given as pledge, that is, early guarantee of this hope.

outline.title: Living by faith and accounting for Christ
outline.explanation: While we remain in the body, we are still absent from the Lord, so we walk by faith and not by sight. Christian trust includes the desire to be with Christ, but also the awareness that we will all attend before the court of Christ, where life in the body will be assessed.

outline.title: Reason for ministry and new way of knowing
outline.explanation: The fear of the Lord and the love of Christ propell Paul's ministry. He does not seek self-promotion, but faithfulness to the gospel. The death of Christ by all implies that those who live must not live for themselves. In Christ, a new creation arises: the old order passed and everything became new.

outline.title: Reconciliation and the righteousness of God in Christ
outline.explanation: All the work comes from God, who has reconciled the world with him through Christ and entrusted to the apostles the word of reconciliation. So they speak as ambassadors, calling people to reconcile with God. The final verse summarizes the gospel: he who knew no sin was made sin for us, that in Christ we might be made righteousness of God.

study.context: The chapter responds to tensions of Paul's ministry and deepens the theme of reconciliation already introduced in the flow of the letter. The text shows that the apostle sees the Christian life from the reality of Christ's death and resurrection, the future hope and the need for a life consistent with the gospel. The notes highlight that the immediate background includes previous sufferings of Paul and the defense of his ministry before the Corinthians.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter brings together eschatology, ethics and soteriology. Christian hope is not mere survival of the soul, but the prospect of a glorified dwelling given by God. The present life is marked by faith, not by vision, and this produces moral seriousness before the court of Christ. The work of Christ redefines identity: his death for all implies replacement, redemptive solidarity and new loyalty, so that the believer lives no longer for himself. Reconciliation is divine, non-human initiative: God acts in Christ to restore the relationship with sinners and entrusted to the church the proclamation of that message. verse 21 is a condensed formulation of atonement and justification: the innocent assumes the condition attached to sin so that the guilty are accepted as righteous in Christ. This reading should be understood as an interpretation of the text and the notes, not as a closed formulation beyond what the chapter says.

scholarViews.insight: Paul's hope is to receive new bodies in the return of the Lord; the groaning of the believer is not a desire to die, but long for the promised transformation.
Paul mentions the court of Christ to awaken the seriousness of the Christian life and to connect future consolation with a present duty.
In "new creature," the point is the real renewal brought by Christ, so that the old condition has passed and a new order of life arises.

questions: How does the hope of an eternal indwelling change the way of facing suffering, aging and death?
What does it mean, in practice, to live by faith and not by the view in concrete decisions of everyday life?
How should the message of reconciliation shape speech, priorities and the testimony of the church?
study.practice: Choose an area in which you have lived more by the view than by faith - for example, fear of the future, need for approval or attachment to the image. Pray this week looking at three truths of the chapter: Christ will return, everyone will account for Him, and God has already begun in you a new creation. Then practice a concrete step of reconciliation: ask for forgiveness, offer forgiveness or proclaim the gospel clearly to someone, with meekness and conviction.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not uniformly detail the meaning of some terms of verse 21; therefore, the expression "sin effect" was treated as sacrificial and representative language, without reducing the text to a single technical formulation. There are also differences in emphasis between the commentators regarding the exact reach of "body," "gemidos" and "new creature," and these differences were preserved as possible interpretations.
